title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 54
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Naming the Places People Live
passages.text:
A. Street names and house numbers feel like a natural feature of a city and are an administrative technology with a traceable purpose. For most of urban history, places were described rather than addressed — the house beside the well, the third door past the baker — which works perfectly among people who know the area and fails entirely for a stranger, a tax collector or anyone attempting to deliver something.

B. Numbering was introduced by states that wanted to find people. The purposes recorded at the time are consistent across countries: taxation, conscription, the billeting of soldiers and the policing of movement, and the schemes were frequently resisted for exactly that reason. Numbers were painted on houses by officials and removed by residents overnight in several documented cases, which is a reasonable response to being made findable by an authority one has reasons to avoid.

C. What made the system useful to residents was a later and different development. Postal delivery, utility connection, emergency services and commercial delivery all require the same capability the tax collector wanted, and once those services existed the address became something people wanted to have rather than something imposed on them. The technology did not change; the balance of who benefited did.

D. The schemes chosen reveal how a city understands itself. Numbering outward from a central point, numbering by distance so that the number indicates how far along a street a building stands, and naming by grid coordinate are all in use, and each makes a different operation easy: finding an unknown address without a map, estimating a walking distance, or expanding the system into new districts without renaming anything.

E. A large proportion of the world's population still lacks a usable address, and the consequences are concrete rather than symbolic. Without one, receiving a delivery, registering for a service, opening a bank account, being found by an ambulance and proving residence for any official purpose all become difficult, and the difficulty falls on informal settlements whose residents are already least able to absorb it.

F. Attempts to solve this with pure geometry have failed for an instructive reason. Systems assigning a unique code to every location on the planet solve the technical problem completely and are not adopted, because an address is a social object as well as a coordinate — people must be able to remember it, say it aloud, recognise approximately where it is, and use it in conversation. A code that satisfies a machine and not a neighbour has solved the smaller half of the problem.

passages.title: The Most Used Solid
passages.text:
Sand is extracted in greater quantity than any other solid material, and almost all of it is used for one purpose: making concrete. A modest building consumes hundreds of tonnes of it, and the scale of construction means the total is measured in tens of billions of tonnes a year — a rate of extraction of a material most people assume to be effectively unlimited because deserts are visibly full of it.

Desert sand is the part of the assumption that fails. Grains transported by wind are rounded and polished by collision, and rounded grains do not lock together, so concrete made with them is weak; what construction requires is angular grains produced by water transport, which occur in rivers, floodplains, lakes and on some coasts. The material is abundant and the useful material is not, and the useful material is concentrated where people already live.

Extraction from rivers causes damage that is out of proportion to its visibility. Removing sand from a riverbed lowers the bed, which steepens the channel, accelerates erosion upstream and downstream, undermines bridge foundations and embankments, and allows salt water further up the channel in coastal reaches. It also removes the habitat of the organisms living in the bed, and the sediment that would have reached and maintained the delta.

Where regulation is weak the extraction is frequently illegal and occasionally violent. The material is bulky, low in value per tonne, and therefore worth taking from close to where it will be used, which means unlicensed operators working near towns; the trade is difficult to police because the product is indistinguishable once delivered, and confrontations over control of extraction sites have caused deaths in several countries.

Substitution is technically possible and constrained by economics rather than by chemistry. Crushed rock produces angular grains suitable for concrete, recycled crushed concrete can replace part of the aggregate, and several industrial by-products can substitute for a proportion of the cement, which reduces the sand required. Each of these costs more than taking sand from a river nearby, which is the entire explanation for their limited use.

The measure that would do most is the one least discussed. A substantial share of the concrete poured is structurally unnecessary — sections oversized because a larger member is cheaper to design than an optimised one, and buildings demolished long before the material has failed — and reducing that waste would cut demand more than any substitute. The constraint is that design time is expensive and material is cheap, which is a pricing problem rather than an engineering one.

passages.title: Small Loans
passages.text:
Lending small sums to people without collateral was long considered impossible, and the demonstration that it could be done with high repayment rates was a genuine discovery. Group lending, in which members guarantee one another, replaced the security a bank normally requires with social pressure and mutual monitoring, and the resulting repayment records were better than those of conventional lending to wealthier borrowers. The finding was real and the conclusions drawn from it went far beyond it.

The claim that followed was that credit alone would lift households out of poverty, and the evidence has not supported it. Randomised evaluations across several countries have consistently found modest effects: some increase in business activity, some change in what households buy, little detectable change in income, consumption, health or schooling. These are not findings of failure — they are findings of a useful financial service that is not a poverty programme.

The reason for the gap is visible in what people borrow for. Much of the lending funds consumption smoothing, a medical bill, school fees or the replacement of a lost asset rather than an enterprise, and this is a sensible use of credit that does not generate the returns needed to escape poverty. A household that borrows to survive a bad month has been helped and has not been made richer.

Interest rates have been the most contested aspect and the arguments on both sides are weaker than they appear. Rates far above commercial bank levels are necessary because administering many tiny loans in dispersed locations is expensive per unit lent, which is a genuine cost rather than exploitation; they are also high enough that a borrower financing consumption at those rates can be made worse off, which is a genuine harm rather than a misunderstanding. Both statements are true simultaneously.

Over-indebtedness is the failure that has caused real damage. In several markets, competing lenders extended multiple loans to the same households without any means of knowing what others had lent, borrowers took new loans to service existing ones, and the resulting crises produced defaults, coercive collection and severe distress. The remedy — shared credit registries — is unglamorous, effective, and was resisted by lenders competing for the same borrowers.

Where the field has moved is towards services other than credit. Savings accounts, payment services and insurance appear in the evidence to do more good than lending for most poor households, and the demand for a safe place to keep money is larger than the demand to borrow. That conclusion is less compelling as a story than the original one, and it is what two decades of measurement produced.
